clue.text: They can afford middle-of-the-road accident protection

definitions.text: They can afford middle-of-the-road accident protection

parts.note: read as bland or moderate in taste, but meant literally: standing in the centre of a street
sounds like an insurance policy, but means a raised refuge sheltering pedestrians from cars

explanation.surface: An advert for an inexpensive, unadventurous insurance policy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Middle-of-the-road' suggests something moderate and 'afford' suggests price; really the clue describes raised kerbed areas in the road centre that give pedestrians safety.
explanation.definitionFit: Raised refuges in the centre of a road shelter people crossing from passing vehicles.

clue.text: Exercise using arms in which one repeatedly aims to improve

definitions.text: Exercise using arms in which one repeatedly aims to improve

parts.note: sounds like a gym workout for the upper body, but arms are weapons here
sounds like general self-betterment, but literally means pointing a gun at a mark over and over

explanation.surface: A description of an arm-strengthening workout done in pursuit of self-improvement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arms' and 'aims' both have a literal firearms meaning hidden under a fitness or self-help reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Shooting repeatedly at a bullseye to sharpen accuracy is the standard drill with firearms or bows.

clue.text: A large demand put on an American separated from others

parts.note: taken as written
to ask is to request or require something
taken as written

explanation.surface: A heavy demand placed on an American who is kept apart from everyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is fair because Alaska is cut off from the rest of the USA by Canada.
explanation.definitionFit: A resident of Alaska is an American from the one mainland state not joined to the other states.

clue.text: Reasonable justification for places of entertainment

parts.note: fair means just or reasonable
grounds are the reasons that justify something

explanation.surface: A sound argument made for opening venues for amusement.
explanation.definitionFit: Fairgrounds are open spaces where funfairs with rides and stalls are set up for amusement.

clue.text: Clever, protecting an old monarch who got wet

indicators.note: the word for clever surrounds the short word as if shielding it

parts.note: cute can mean shrewd or clever, as in a cute move
taken as written

explanation.surface: A smart guard keeps an elderly king safe after he has been soaked.
explanation.walkthrough: King Canute (Cnut) is said to have sat on the shore and failed to command the tide to halt.
explanation.definitionFit: The legend of the eleventh-century king of England who ordered back the waves ends with his feet wet.

clue.text: Directions on youngster's examination from which height is determined

parts.note: south and east, two compass points
A level is the English school exam taken at about eighteen

explanation.surface: The instructions written on a teenager's exam paper used to decide their position.
explanation.walkthrough: A levels are the British exams taken in the final years of school, before university.
explanation.definitionFit: Altitudes and heights of mountains are measured relative to the mean surface of the sea.

clue.text: A part of circle that's central? Yes and no

definitions.text: A part of circle that's central? Yes and no

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: only the middle letters of the word for the round shape are kept

parts.note: the word circle has six letters, and its two central ones are kept

explanation.surface: A puzzled question whether a curved section of a ring lies at its centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yes and no' admits the joke: the answer is a part of a circle and its central letters, but a curve on the rim is not central.
explanation.definitionFit: An arc is a portion of the circumference of a circle, a curved segment of its edge.

clue.text: Son located in OK lineage

indicators.note: the son's letter is placed within the word for acceptable

parts.note: decent means acceptable or passable

explanation.surface: A son traced back to a family line from Oklahoma.
explanation.walkthrough: 'OK' looks like the state abbreviation; it means satisfactory.
explanation.definitionFit: Descent means ancestry or family origin, the line a person is born into.

clue.text: Practice session players are fully kitted out for

definitions.text: Practice session players are fully kitted out for

parts.note: sounds like a sports team, but means actors in a theatre
sounds like sports kit, but means wearing complete stage costume

explanation.surface: A training session for which a team turns up in full kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Players' and 'kitted out' point to sport; the session is the final theatre run-through in costume.
explanation.definitionFit: The last full run-through of a play before opening night, performed in costume as if for an audience.

clue.text: Rule about a learner put in new group

indicators.note: the word for rule goes around the other letters, holding them inside it

parts.note: to reign is to rule as a monarch
taken as written
L is the learner-driver plate letter

explanation.surface: A new ruling sees a trainee moved into a different team.
explanation.definitionFit: To realign is to rearrange things or people into a fresh arrangement or alliance.

clue.text: Prosecutor in case tangled with RUC

indicators.note: the two words are knotted together so their letters come out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A prosecuting lawyer in a court case clashes with the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
explanation.walkthrough: The RUC was the Royal Ulster Constabulary, Northern Ireland's former police force.
explanation.definitionFit: An accuser is one who brings a charge against someone, which is what a prosecutor does.

clue.text: You may see them in Yellowstone National Park, finally

definitions.text: You may see them in Yellowstone National Park, finally

indicators.note: the closing letter of each of the three park words is taken

parts.note: the three words end in the letters wanted, one from each

explanation.surface: A tourist note on what wildlife a visitor can spot in the famous American park.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: the animals really do roam the park.
explanation.definitionFit: These large deer, also called wapiti, are among the best-known animals living in that national park.

clue.text: It's good, say, to hold down sensation-mongers

parts.note: to utter is to say aloud
to press is to push something down and keep it there

explanation.surface: A seemingly moral claim that it is right to silence those who peddle scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' is not an example marker here but a verb in its own right.
explanation.definitionFit: Tabloid newspapers that trade in scandal and lurid stories are called this, as they peddle sensation.

clue.text: Part of pitch in which a neat player gets fouled

indicators.note: the phrase is roughed up and its letters thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A tidy footballer is brought down by an opponent in a particular zone of the field.
explanation.definitionFit: The marked box in front of each goal on a football field is where fouls lead to spot-kicks.

clue.text: Attach atom, more or less, for a bit of a lark, say

definitions.text: a bit of a lark, say

parts.note: to pin something is to fasten it on
an ion is an atom that has gained or lost electrons, so nearly an atom

explanation.surface: Instructions to fix an atom onto something as part of a playful prank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lark' pretends to mean a bit of fun; it is the bird, and 'say' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A pinion is the outer part of a bird's wing, so it is a portion of a songbird such as a lark.

clue.text: Re-enlist in irregular formation in part of Ireland

indicators.note: the letters are drawn up out of their usual order, like troops in a ragged line

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A soldier signs up again and is posted to a scruffy unit somewhere in Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Leinster is one of the four historic provinces of Ireland, in the east and including Dublin.

clue.text: Husband still superficially smooth?

parts.note: airless means without a breeze, so calm and still

explanation.surface: A wife's question about whether her spouse's skin is still soft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' looks like the adverb meaning yet; it is the adjective meaning calm.
explanation.definitionFit: Having no hair makes skin smooth to the touch on its surface, as with a bald head.

clue.text: Foreign citizen taking three articles around part of UK

indicators.note: the three little words sit on either side of the abbreviation, wrapping it

parts.note: the English articles a, the and an, run together
NI is Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: An overseas national carrying three items of luggage around a corner of Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' suggests objects, but here it means grammatical articles. The abbreviation lands between the second and third.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Athens is a citizen of the Greek capital, hence a foreign national from a British viewpoint.

clue.text: He would admit band inside for country dance

indicators.note: the ring shape goes within the shortened form of he would

parts.note: he'd, shortened and with the apostrophe dropped
O is a ring-shaped band
to own is to confess, as in own up

explanation.surface: A man says he'd let a group of musicians in to play for a barn dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' looks like musicians, but it is a ring, shaped like the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoedown is a lively American folk gathering with square dancing, a rural social dance.

clue.text: Looking slightly bruised, quite near the knuckle?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: tinged with blue, as a bruise is
second meaning: somewhat risqué, since blue jokes are smutty ones

explanation.walkthrough: 'Near the knuckle' is a British idiom for a joke that is close to being indecent; 'blue' means the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Somewhat blue in colour describes a bruise, and somewhat blue in humour describes a mildly rude joke.

clue.text: Firmly fix in the middle of menacing rainstorm

indicators.note: the letters sit within the run of the two words, across their join

parts.note: the run of letters straddles the end of menacing and the start of rainstorm

explanation.surface: Someone must secure something tightly while a threatening downpour rages.
explanation.definitionFit: To ingrain something is to embed it deeply so that it is hard to remove, as with a habit.

clue.text: Language football team pronounced differently at first

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a branch of languages such as Welsh and Gaelic, said with a hard K sound
second meaning: the Glasgow club, said with a soft S sound

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pronounced differently at first' points out that the opening sound changes between the two senses. Celtic is a famous Scottish football club based in Glasgow.
explanation.definitionFit: The same word names a family of tongues including Irish and Welsh and a leading Scottish football club.

clue.text: Medical treatment for elders, for example?

definitions.text: Medical treatment for elders, for example?

parts.note: sounds like care for patients, but means pruning and repairing timber plants
seems to mean old people, but elders are shrubs or small trees

explanation.surface: Healthcare provided to senior citizens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elders' looks like the elderly, but the elder is a flowering shrub whose berries make wine.
explanation.definitionFit: The skilled cutting and care of damaged or diseased woody plants by an arborist.

clue.text: Home of some Indians in Georgia or Alabama, originally

indicators.note: the opening letter of each of the three words is taken, as their origin

parts.note: the three words begin with the letters wanted, one from each

explanation.surface: A history note that some Native Americans first lived in two southern US states.
explanation.walkthrough: The American states make you think of Native Americans, but the Indians are from India.
explanation.definitionFit: Goa is a small state on the west coast of India, so it is where some people of India live.

clue.text: Nice thing to eat on hot day that's excellent, cold inside

definitions.text: Nice thing to eat on hot day

indicators.note: the abbreviation for cold goes within the word for excellent

parts.note: choice can mean of very good quality, as in choice cuts

explanation.surface: A recommendation for a cool, top-quality snack on a sweltering day.
explanation.walkthrough: A choc-ice is a British treat: a bar of ice cream coated in chocolate.
explanation.definitionFit: A chocolate-coated ice cream bar is a welcome cold snack to enjoy when the weather is hot.

clue.text: Bad state Chicago is in, in short

definitions.text: state Chicago is in, in short
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the abbreviated form of Illinois, the US state containing Chicago

explanation.walkthrough: 'In short' marks an abbreviation: Ill. is the traditional short form of Illinois.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means poor or unwell, and is also the old postal shortening for the state of Illinois.

clue.text: Dangers in attempts to heal outside hospital

indicators.note: the word for healing attempts stands around the hospital letter

parts.note: a doctor treats a patient in trying to cure them

explanation.surface: Risks arise when doctors try to cure patients away from a hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: Threats are menaces or hazards, things that put someone at risk.

clue.text: Something viewed by many here as what divides us from Europe

definitions.text: Something viewed by many here as what divides us from Europe

parts.words: Something viewed by many here as what divides us from Europe
parts.note: plays on viewed as watched, like a television station, and viewed as regarded, the sea that many Britons see as their barrier from the Continent

explanation.surface: A wry comment on how many Britons see the sea as cutting them off from Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Viewed' has two senses: watched like TV, and regarded as. Both fit a sea that sounds like a broadcaster.
explanation.definitionFit: The narrow sea between southern England and northern France is what separates Britain from mainland Europe.
